questions.question: What is the difference between include and extend in Ruby?
questions.title: Include vs Extend
questions.direct_answer: `include SomeModule` makes the module's instance methods available to instances of the receiving class, while `extend SomeModule` makes those methods singleton methods of the receiving object. Therefore `User.include(Greeting)` lets `User.new.greet` work; `User.extend(Greeting)` lets `User.greet` work. Any individual object can also be extended without changing other instances of its class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know include = instance methods and extend = class/singleton methods.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using include when you wanted class methods (use extend), or expecting extend to affect instances.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: include = instance methods (C.new has them); extend = class/singleton methods (C has them, or one obj). include for mixins; extend for class helpers.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `include M` gives a class's instances access to `M`'s instance methods.
- `extend M` gives the receiving object access to those methods directly.
- Extending a class creates class-level behaviour because the class is an object.
- Extending one instance affects that object, not every instance of its class.
- Choose by asking which receiver should answer the method call.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Both `include` and `extend` reuse instance methods from a module. The difference is who receives those methods. `include Greeting` inside `User` makes `greet` available to User instances, so the call is `User.new.greet`. `User.extend(Greeting)` adds it to the User class object, so the call is `User.greet`.

Use `include` when the behaviour belongs to every instance, such as each invoice being printable. Use `extend` on a class when the type itself should perform the operation, such as `Invoice.from_csv(data)`. This is why Ruby modules can provide either instance behaviour or class-level helpers without inheritance.

The module below defines one ordinary instance method. `Member` includes it, while `Team` extends itself with it. The method body is the same, but `self` is whichever object receives the call.

Neither operation copies the module's own state into the receiver. The reused method runs with the receiver as `self` and can therefore use that receiver's instance variables. Extending one object, as in `report.extend(DebugLabels)`, affects only that object. Keep a mixin focused on one clear capability so its required state is easy to understand.

support.title: Include for instances; extend for the class
support.code:
module Greeting
  def greeting_target
    self
  end
end

class Member
  include Greeting
end

class Team
  extend Greeting
end

puts Member.new.greeting_target.class
puts Team.greeting_target
support.caption: Output: `Member`, then `Team`. The receiver changes even though the module method stays the same.

beats.recallRule: Ask who should receive the call: an instance means `include`; the class or one object means `extend`.

sections.title: Include, extend, and the method lookup chain
sections.content:
A module stores instance-method definitions. `include` inserts that module into the ancestor chain used by instances of the class. Ruby still performs normal message lookup; it does not paste a second independent copy of each method into every object.

`extend` operates on one receiver. It includes the module in that receiver's singleton class, a hidden class that holds methods unique to the object. When the receiver happens to be a class object, those singleton methods are what Ruby developers normally call class methods.

This model explains why `obj.extend(M)` is local to `obj` and why module methods can read the receiver's state. Inside the reused method, `self` is the object that received the call—not the module where the method was written.

Hooks can combine both ideas, but a beginner-facing design often stays clearer with an explicit `include InstanceMethods` and `extend ClassMethods`. A module should express one coherent capability; using it only to avoid typing a few unrelated methods hides dependencies rather than improving design.

sections.title: The receiver decides between include and extend
sections.content:
| Declaration | Method call that works | Where the module enters lookup |
|---|---|---|
| `class User; include Greeting; end` | `User.new.greet` | User instances' ancestor chain |
| `class User; extend Greeting; end` | `User.greet` | User object's singleton class |
| `user.extend(Greeting)` | `user.greet` | That one user's singleton class |

sections.title: The same module can serve three different receivers
sections.content:
```ruby
module Greeting
  def greet
    "hello from #{self.class}"
  end
end

class Member
  include Greeting
end
Member.new.greet             # => 'hello from Member'

class Team
  extend Greeting
end
Team.greet                   # => 'hello from Class'

guest = Object.new
guest.extend(Greeting)
guest.greet                  # only guest gained this method
```
